newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Ethiopian former minister charged with corruption.
newsitem.headline: Ethiopian former minister charged with corruption.

text.p: Former Ethiopian Deputy Prime Minister Tamirat Layne and eight others were charged on Thursday with abuse of office and involvement in corruption scandals in which millions of dollars were lost.

Tamirat, also a former defence minister, and the others were brought to the court in Addis Ababa under heavy security escort of plain-clothed policemen and Criminal Investigations Department officers. They appeared relaxed and in good health.

Tamirat was prime minister during Ethiopia's transition period from 1991 to 1994. He became deputy prime minister later in 1994 when president Meles Zenawi became prime minister under a new federal constitution. The prosecution says Tamirat abused power both as prime minister and deputy prime minister.
He was sacked in October and put under protective custody.
The nine were not required to enter their pleas. They face prison terms of between three and 15 years if found guilty. Those charged with Tamirat include his former secretary and businessmen.
Tamirat, 42, came to the Federal Supreme Court dressed in a double-breasted grey coat, black trouser and white shirt. He did not wear a tie.
He calmly stood in the dock with the other accused.
A seven-page charge sheet by the prosecution accused Tamirat and the others of gross abuse of power and corruption.

It said in the first count that Tamirat, a prime minister during Ethiopia's transition period, abused his office and entered into an illegal $16 million deal with a business firm that sought distribution of textile goods in Ethiopia.

It said the firm transferred $9 million from a New York account to Tamirat's bank account in London; Tamirat kept $5 million in London and transferred $500,000 to the Switzerland bank account of his four-year-old son Belen Getachew Mamo.

Tamirat transferred a further $2.5 million to Djibouti-based Ramis International Company that he owned and then allegedly gave $1 million to Nadia Kassim, one of the accused and not present in court on Thursday, the charge documents said.
No indication was given as to what happened to the balance of $7 million from the total of $16 million.
Tamirat was also accused of using his position to export 1,000 tonnes of state coffee through a bogus firm for $3.6 million and taking $1.8 million of the proceeds for himself.

On another count, prosecutors accused Tamirat of fraudulently obtaining a tender for the supply of construction equipment worth 67 million birr ($11 million). It did not state his personal gain from the tender.
Prosecutors also charged Tamirat with using is power to award a tender for the resurfacing of a major highway.
The court refused bail for all the accused and the trial was adjourned for April 15 to give the accused time to study the charges and also appoint their defence lawyers.
